---

Title: [[Archæology Of Media]]

question
How can we study the contribution of media to culture and society without presupposing a single, totalizing theory of culture?

claim
An “archæology of media” investigates each communicative event by tracing the recursive and iterative media operations that embed it in morphograms and kenograms, accepting that only partial “boreholes” are ever possible and analysis is, in Freud’s sense, potentially endless.

support
Baecker proposes a media archæology that asks, for each event of communication, action, or experience, which chains of media operations (writing, images, money, law, technical devices, etc.) recursively frame and re-frame it. He uses Günther’s terminology of morphograms (patterned forms) and kenograms (empty places) to formalize this. 

support
This archæology is principledly local: only “Einzelbohrungen” (single drillings) are possible, and different starting points would yield different reconstructions. This matches Foucault’s notion of archæology as tracing positivity and singularities rather than reconstructing a hidden whole.

support
The media archæology is explicitly tied to culture as the double circuit of society: media enable condensation and forgetting of Widerstreit, but also carry the traces that can be reactivated in Negativsprachen and cultural critique.

oppose
A critical stance might find this too text- and symbol-centric, arguing that infrastructures (roads, power grids, logistics, bodies) need an “archæology” that is not easily captured in semiotic or morphogrammatic terms.

oppose
Empirically, the demand to trace all recursive and iterative media chains may be infeasible beyond micro-cases; the method risks becoming a beautiful but paralyzing ideal.
